title: Earth Events
description: Earth's surface is changed by earthquakes, volcanoes, erosion, and other events. Some changes are rapid, others occur over millions of years. Scientists classify changes as fast or slow.

exercises.question: Which is an example of a FAST change to Earth's surface?
choices: a river slowly cutting a canyon over millions of years
a volcanic eruption covering land in lava within hours
mountains slowly rising over millions of years
glaciers carving valleys over thousands of years
exercises.exp: Volcanic eruptions happen very quickly — lava flows can travel kilometres in hours, changing the landscape fast!

exercises.question: Which is an example of a SLOW change to Earth's surface?
choices: a tsunami flooding a coastline
a landslide
erosion by a river carving rock over millions of years
an earthquake cracking a road
exercises.exp: River erosion is very slow — the Grand Canyon took about 5–6 million years for the Colorado River to carve!

exercises.question: What evidence might you find that shows a LANDSLIDE occurred?
choices: a new mountain appeared overnight
a slope covered in debris with uprooted trees and displaced soil
a flat plain formed over millions of years
a new river channel
exercises.exp: Landslide evidence: slopes covered in fallen rock and soil, uprooted trees, and blocked valley floors.

exercises.question: EARTHQUAKES are caused by ___.
choices: heavy rainfall
tectonic plates (pieces of Earth's crust) suddenly moving and releasing energy
volcanoes always
human construction
exercises.exp: Tectonic plates move slowly. When they suddenly slip or grind past each other, energy is released as earthquake shaking!

exercises.question: What is the EPICENTRE of an earthquake?
choices: the deepest point underground where the quake starts
the point on Earth's surface directly above where the earthquake starts
the largest building damaged
the city hit hardest
exercises.exp: The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus (where the quake starts underground).

exercises.question: Lava from a VOLCANO cools and hardens into ___.
choices: sedimentary rock
metamorphic rock
igneous rock
fossil rock
exercises.exp: Cooled lava forms igneous rock (like basalt and granite). Hawaii is made mostly of igneous rock from volcanoes!

exercises.question: Which agent causes erosion of coastal cliffs?
choices: underground heat
ocean waves constantly hitting the cliff face
wind only
earthquakes only
exercises.exp: Ocean waves batter cliffs with tremendous force, slowly breaking off pieces — coastal erosion!

exercises.question: A glacier ERODES the land by ___.
choices: heating and melting rock
scraping, grinding, and carrying rock as it slowly moves
dropping sediment in layers
splitting rock with lightning
exercises.exp: Glaciers are like massive slow bulldozers — as they move, they scrape and grind the land beneath them.

exercises.question: A scientist finds folded and bent rock layers. What might have caused this?
choices: water erosion
a landslide
powerful tectonic forces pushing rock layers over millions of years
a meteorite impact only
exercises.exp: Folded rock layers show evidence of massive compression forces from tectonic plate movement — like a giant slow squeeze!

exercises.question: DEPOSITION is the process where ___.
choices: rocks are broken apart by water
sediment is carried away by water
sediment is dropped and builds up in a new location
volcanoes form new rock
exercises.exp: Deposition happens when water or wind slow down and drop the sediment they were carrying — building new landforms!

exercises.question: After a VOLCANIC ERUPTION, new land can be created when ___.
choices: rain washes away old land
lava flows into the ocean and cools into new solid rock
earthquakes move land around
glaciers carve new channels
exercises.exp: Hawaii's Big Island is still growing today — lava flows into the ocean and cools into new igneous rock, adding new land!

exercises.question: What do scientists use to MEASURE the strength of an earthquake?
choices: a thermometer
a barometer
the Richter scale (or Moment Magnitude scale)
a rain gauge
exercises.exp: The Richter scale (or modern Moment Magnitude scale) measures earthquake strength — each point is 10× more energy!

exercises.question: SEISMIC WAVES spread out from an earthquake's focus. Why do buildings farther away feel less shaking?
choices: seismic waves only travel in one direction
waves lose energy as they travel through Earth's crust — the farther from the epicentre, the weaker the shaking
buildings farther away are stronger
earthquakes stop at city boundaries
exercises.exp: Like ripples in water, seismic waves spread out and lose energy with distance. Areas near the epicentre feel strong shaking; distant areas feel gentle tremors.

exercises.question: CONTINENTAL DRIFT is the theory that ___.
choices: continents have always been in their current positions
the continents were once joined together and have slowly moved apart over hundreds of millions of years
continents drift into the ocean eventually
only small landmasses drift
exercises.exp: Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents fit together like puzzle pieces and have drifted apart over 200+ million years — now supported by extensive evidence!

exercises.question: Which is the BEST evidence that continents were once JOINED?
choices: all continents have similar climates
identical fossils of the same organisms are found on different continents that are now separated by oceans
all continents have the same flag
continents are the same size
exercises.exp: Mesosaurus fossils found in both Brazil and West Africa (now separated by the Atlantic) suggest they were once joined — the same creature could not have crossed the ocean!

exercises.question: TECTONIC PLATES move about 2–5 cm per year — about as fast as your FINGERNAILS grow. How does this slow movement cause big changes?
choices: it cannot cause big changes — it is too slow
over millions of years, even tiny movements accumulate — mountains rise, oceans open, and continents drift thousands of kilometres
fast movements happen sometimes, slow never
plate movement only affects the ocean floor
exercises.exp: Geological time is vast. 2 cm/year × 50 million years = 1000 km of movement! Mountains, ocean basins, and continents result from these slow but relentless forces.

exercises.question: A SUBDUCTION ZONE forms when ___.
choices: two plates move apart
one tectonic plate slides under another, diving into the mantle
two plates collide head-on and both rise
plates move sideways past each other
exercises.exp: Where oceanic plates meet continental plates, the denser oceanic plate dives (subducts) under the lighter continental plate into the mantle — creating deep ocean trenches and volcanic arcs!

exercises.question: The PACIFIC RING OF FIRE has frequent earthquakes and volcanoes because ___.
choices: it is hotter near the equator
it follows the edges of tectonic plates around the Pacific Ocean where plates collide, separate, and subduct
it is near the North Pole
Pacific water is more volcanic
exercises.exp: The Ring of Fire traces the Pacific plate's boundaries — where plates grind, collide, and subduct. About 90% of world's earthquakes and 75% of active volcanoes occur here!

exercises.question: LAVA TUBES form when ___.
choices: magma melts tunnels underground
the outer surface of a lava flow cools and hardens while hot lava continues flowing inside, then drains out leaving a hollow tube
water creates tunnels in lava rocks
earthquakes split lava into tubes
exercises.exp: The outer shell hardens into rock while molten lava keeps flowing inside. When it drains, a hollow tube remains — sometimes kilometres long! Hawaii has famous lava tubes.

exercises.question: VOLCANIC ASH can travel THOUSANDS of kilometres in the atmosphere. What effect does this have?
choices: it only affects the area around the volcano
ash particles block sunlight worldwide, causing temporary cooling and disrupting aviation, agriculture, and air quality far away
volcanic ash improves air quality
ash is too heavy to travel far
exercises.exp: The 1991 Pinatubo eruption cooled Earth by 0.5°C for 2 years! Ash spread globally, causing spectacular sunsets. Ash also closes airports and damages aircraft engines.

exercises.question: Why does SOIL form on top of volcanic rock QUICKLY (geologically)?
choices: volcanic rock is pre-made soil
volcanic minerals are rich in nutrients — they weather rapidly and combine with organic matter to form fertile soil
soil only forms on non-volcanic rocks
plants cannot grow on volcanic rock at all
exercises.exp: Volcanic rock weathers into mineral-rich soil relatively quickly. Pioneer plants colonise it, die, and add organic matter. Hawaiian and Icelandic volcanic soils are remarkably fertile!

exercises.question: FLOODS can change Earth's surface by ___.
choices: only damaging buildings
depositing large amounts of sediment that can build up riverbanks and floodplains, or erode existing land
floods have no lasting effect on landforms
only removing trees
exercises.exp: Major floods deposit huge amounts of sediment — building up fertile floodplains (like the Nile delta) or carving new channels. The 2011 Queensland floods reshaped parts of Australia.

exercises.question: How does WIND EROSION differ from WATER EROSION?
choices: they are identical processes
wind erosion occurs in dry areas with loose, unprotected soil — carrying fine particles; water erosion is driven by flowing water cutting through rock and soil
wind erosion is faster than water erosion always
water cannot erode rock — only wind can
exercises.exp: Wind erosion dominates in dry deserts and bare areas; water erosion dominates where rain falls and rivers flow. Both break down and move material, but by very different mechanisms.

exercises.question: THE DUST BOWL (1930s North America) was a massive WIND EROSION disaster caused by ___.
choices: a volcanic eruption
deep ploughing of prairie grasses combined with severe drought — exposed topsoil was blown away in massive dust storms
flooding that removed topsoil
an earthquake that loosened the soil
exercises.exp: Prairie grasses had held soil for millennia. When ploughed up and drought struck, there was nothing to hold the exposed topsoil — black blizzards of dust buried farms and caused mass migration.

exercises.question: CHEMICAL WEATHERING is when rock is broken down by ___.
choices: physical force like hammers and glaciers
chemical reactions with water, acids, or oxygen (like rust and acid rain dissolving limestone)
earthquakes cracking rocks
roots physically splitting rocks
exercises.exp: Chemical weathering chemically alters rock — carbonic acid (rainwater + CO₂) dissolves limestone creating caves. Oxygen rusts iron minerals. Chemical changes break down rock composition.

exercises.question: PHYSICAL WEATHERING breaks rock into smaller pieces WITHOUT changing its chemical composition. Which is an example?
choices: acid rain dissolving limestone
oxygen rusting iron minerals in rock
water freezing in cracks and expanding, splitting rock apart
salt water chemically reacting with minerals
exercises.exp: Ice wedging is classic physical weathering — water enters cracks, freezes, expands with 9% more volume, and pries the crack wider. Eventually the rock splits — purely physical!

exercises.question: CAVES in limestone areas are formed by ___.
choices: physical erosion by rivers
rainwater slightly acidified by CO₂ slowly dissolving limestone over thousands of years (chemical weathering)
volcanic activity melting limestone
underground earthquakes creating voids
exercises.exp: Slightly acidic rainwater (carbonic acid = CO₂ + H₂O) slowly dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone — carving caves, sinkholes, and karst landscapes over thousands of years.

exercises.question: What evidence do scientists use to understand Earth's INTERNAL STRUCTURE?
choices: drilling to the centre of Earth
analysing how seismic waves travel through Earth — different layers change wave speed and direction
looking inside active volcanoes
measuring gravity only
exercises.exp: We cannot drill to Earth's centre — we use seismology! Seismic waves bend, speed up, and slow down at boundaries between layers. This revealed Earth's crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core!

exercises.question: SOIL FORMATION (pedogenesis) is very SLOW. It takes about 1000 years to form 1 cm of topsoil. Why is this significant?
choices: soil is easy to replace quickly
topsoil lost to erosion takes millennia to reform — protecting soil is critical for food security and ecosystem health
1 cm of soil is not very important
soil formation can be accelerated by machines easily
exercises.exp: We erode soil in decades that took centuries to form. Once topsoil is gone, farming becomes nearly impossible for generations. Soil conservation is one of agriculture's most important challenges!

exercises.question: PLATE BOUNDARIES are classified as CONVERGENT, DIVERGENT, or TRANSFORM. Which causes the least dramatic surface changes?
choices: convergent boundaries where plates collide
divergent boundaries where plates spread apart (like mid-ocean ridges)
transform boundaries where plates slide sideways past each other
all cause equally dramatic changes
exercises.exp: Transform boundaries (like the San Andreas Fault) — plates grinding past each other — cause major earthquakes but little volcanic activity and relatively slow surface change compared to convergent or divergent boundaries.

exercises.question: TSUNAMIS can travel across entire OCEANS. What do they look like in deep water?
choices: massive 30-metre waves visible from aircraft
very long, low waves only about 1 metre high but moving at 800 km/h — barely noticeable at sea
they look like foam on the surface
they appear as spinning whirlpools
exercises.exp: In deep water, tsunamis are low but incredibly fast (800 km/h). Their wavelength can be hundreds of km. They only pile up into towering destructive waves as they enter shallow coastal water!

exercises.question: What type of volcano erupts explosively with thick, sticky lava and produces a lot of ash?
choices: shield volcano — broad, gently sloping, runny lava
composite volcano (stratovolcano) — steep-sided, explosive, thick lava, lots of ash
cinder cone — low, small, single eruption
lava dome — small and dome-shaped
exercises.exp: Composite/stratovolcanoes (like Mount St. Helens, Mount Fuji) have silica-rich, viscous lava that traps gases — building pressure until explosive eruptions!

exercises.question: What is LIQUEFACTION during an earthquake?
choices: rocks melting from seismic heat
water-saturated soil temporarily losing strength and behaving like liquid during shaking — buildings can sink or tilt
lava flowing from volcanic eruptions
ice melting from seismic vibrations
exercises.exp: Liquefaction: seismic shaking causes water-saturated, loosely packed soil to lose its solid structure and flow like liquid. Buildings literally sink into the ground. Common near coastlines!

exercises.question: SEISMIC WAVES travel through Earth in different ways. P-waves (primary) ___.
choices: only travel through liquids
travel through solids and liquids as compression waves — the fastest seismic waves
travel along Earth's surface only
travel in S-patterns and are slower than S-waves
exercises.exp: P-waves (compression waves) travel through any medium (solid, liquid, gas) and arrive first. S-waves (shear waves) travel only through solids. Scientists use this to study Earth's layers!

exercises.question: S-WAVES cannot travel through Earth's outer core. This tells us ___.
choices: the outer core does not exist
the outer core is made of solid rock
the outer core must be LIQUID — S-waves cannot pass through liquids
all seismic waves are blocked by the core
exercises.exp: S-wave shadow zones prove the outer core is liquid. S-waves only travel through solids. The fact that they disappear beyond certain angles proves the outer core is molten iron!

exercises.question: After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami warning systems were improved. These systems use ___.
choices: weather satellites only
seismographs to detect undersea earthquakes + ocean buoys to detect wave changes → alert coastal populations before waves arrive
radio signals from volcanoes
aircraft monitoring ocean surfaces
exercises.exp: Tsunami Early Warning Systems: seismographs detect undersea quakes; DART buoys detect pressure changes from waves; alerts go out within minutes to give coastal populations time to evacuate!

exercises.question: Why do VOLCANIC ERUPTIONS sometimes cause TSUNAMIS?
choices: volcanic gases cool the ocean forming ice tsunamis
underwater volcanic eruptions or volcanic island collapses displace huge volumes of water, generating tsunami waves
volcanic ash makes ocean water denser, causing waves
volcanic heat boils water causing steam-driven waves
exercises.exp: Underwater eruptions and caldera collapses displace enormous water volumes → tsunamis! The 1883 Krakatoa eruption generated 30-metre waves; the 2022 Tonga eruption caused a Pacific-wide tsunami.

exercises.question: AFTERSHOCKS occur after a major earthquake because ___.
choices: a second earthquake happens nearby by coincidence
the rocks around the fault continue adjusting to the new stress distribution created by the main quake
aftershocks only happen within 1 hour
they are caused by falling buildings hitting the ground
exercises.exp: After the main shock, surrounding rock is stressed and unstable — it continues adjusting through a series of smaller earthquakes (aftershocks). Major quakes can produce aftershocks for months/years!

exercises.question: Which scale do modern seismologists use to measure earthquake energy?
choices: Richter Scale (still used, but limited)
Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw) — measures total energy released, accurate for all earthquake sizes
Beaufort Scale
Fujita Scale
exercises.exp: The Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw) replaced Richter for scientific use — it accurately measures energy for all sizes. The 2011 Japan earthquake was Mw 9.0 — the most powerful in Japan's recorded history.

exercises.question: VOLCANIC GASES released during eruptions include mainly ___.
choices: only oxygen
only carbon dioxide
water vapour, CO₂, SO₂, and hydrogen sulfide — some toxic, some climate-affecting
pure nitrogen only
exercises.exp: Volcanic gases: mostly water vapour (60-90%), CO₂, SO₂, and H₂S. SO₂ causes acid rain; large eruptions inject aerosols that cool climate. These gases also contributed to early Earth's atmosphere!

exercises.question: A CALDERA is ___.
choices: a small volcanic cone
a large depression formed when a volcano's magma chamber empties and the summit collapses inward
the vent at a volcano's tip
the zone around a volcano affected by lava flows only
exercises.exp: Calderas form when massive eruptions empty the magma chamber → roof collapses → enormous circular depression. Yellowstone is a supervolcano caldera! Crater Lake, Oregon formed this way.

exercises.question: Earthquakes along the San Andreas Fault occur because the Pacific and North American plates ___.
choices: are moving toward each other (convergent)
are moving apart (divergent)
are sliding past each other (transform fault)
are stationary but vibrating
exercises.exp: The San Andreas is a right-lateral strike-slip (transform) fault — the Pacific Plate moves NW relative to the North American Plate. The plates grind past each other, producing frequent earthquakes.

exercises.question: Why is PREDICTING exact earthquake timing so difficult?
choices: seismographs are not sensitive enough
earthquakes are completely random and unpredictable
rock systems are complex and chaotic — we can identify HIGH-RISK zones but not when or exactly where a future quake will strike
scientists simply have not tried to predict earthquakes
exercises.exp: Earthquake prediction is one of science's greatest challenges. Stress builds in rocks over decades but releases suddenly at unpredictable moments. We identify hazard zones but cannot give exact predictions.

exercises.question: What is PYROCLASTIC FLOW?
choices: slow lava creeping down a slope
a fast-moving mixture of hot gas, ash, and volcanic rock fragments that flows down a volcano's slope at up to 700 km/h, destroying everything in its path
a river of cooled volcanic rock
a cloud of acid rain from a volcano
exercises.exp: Pyroclastic flows are the most dangerous volcanic hazard — a superheated avalanche of gas, ash, and rock at up to 700 km/h. The 79 AD Vesuvius eruption buried Pompeii in pyroclastic surges!

exercises.question: Why do VOLCANIC ISLANDS form chains (like Hawaii)?
choices: they form at random locations in the ocean
volcanoes form a straight line along a mid-ocean ridge only
a tectonic plate moves over a fixed hot spot in the mantle — each new position produces a new volcano, creating a chain with the oldest island furthest away
islands form from coral reefs growing upward over time
exercises.exp: Hot spot + moving plate = island chain! Hawaiian islands age progressively — Hawaii (youngest, still active) to Kauai (oldest, most eroded). The plate moved NW over a fixed mantle hot spot.

exercises.question: Geothermal energy harnesses heat from ___.
choices: the sun's radiation reaching underground
burning coal underground
Earth's internal heat (from radioactive decay and original planetary formation energy) accessed via steam and hot water from deep in the crust
chemical reactions in soil
exercises.exp: Geothermal energy: Earth's internal heat drives steam that spins turbines. Iceland gets 66% of its energy from geothermal. It is renewable, low-carbon, and available 24/7 in volcanic regions!

exercises.question: A SUPERVOLCANO eruption (like Yellowstone if it erupted) would be different from a regular eruption because ___.
choices: it would only affect the local area
it would last exactly one day
it would release thousands of times more material, injecting enough ash and aerosols into the atmosphere to cool global climate for years (volcanic winter)
it would be the same as a regular eruption but in a more populated area
exercises.exp: A supervolcano eruption (VEI 8) ejects 1000+ km³ of material. Ash blankets continents; aerosols cause years of global cooling and crop failures. The Toba eruption (74,000 years ago) may have nearly wiped out humans!

exercises.question: The MODIFIED MERCALLI SCALE measures ___.
choices: earthquake energy (same as Richter)
the INTENSITY of shaking at a specific location — based on observed effects on people, buildings, and the ground (I to XII)
the depth of the earthquake focus
the speed of tectonic plate movement
exercises.exp: Mercalli scale measures shaking intensity at a location (how violently things shake). An earthquake has ONE magnitude (energy) but DIFFERENT intensities at different distances. Essential for damage assessment!

exercises.question: Which human activities can TRIGGER earthquakes?
choices: growing crops
deep mining, reservoir impoundment (water weight), and hydraulic fracturing (fracking) can trigger earthquakes by stressing or lubricating fault zones
using solar panels
building wooden houses
exercises.exp: Induced seismicity: fracking and wastewater injection from oil extraction have triggered thousands of earthquakes in Oklahoma, USA. Reservoir water weight has triggered significant earthquakes too!
